title: The monk Dharmakara
hookLine: a monk in the distant past makes his vows to create a land where all can awaken (Larger Sukhavati-vyuha)

cards: A king sits in a crowd, listening to a Buddha teach.

It's a story the Buddha tells his attendant Ananda in the longer sutra on the land of bliss, set in ages so far back the sutra stacks one past age on another to reach it. The Buddha teaching is named Lokeshvararaja.
The king hears him, and something lands so deep that he gives up his throne, takes the robe, and becomes a monk. His new name is Dharmakara. And this monk is about to ask for something enormous.

teach.b: First, the change. A king becomes a monk, and that's the whole pattern in miniature: giving up one kind of power to take on another kind of work. Second, the request.
Dharmakara asks his teacher to show him the lands of the Buddhas, the fine and the poor, so he can make a land of his own that gathers up what's best. His teacher shows him.
Then the monk goes quiet, and in the sutra he spends an immense stretch of time thinking it through before he says a word. Third, the vows.

teach.h: IF NOT, MAY I NOT AWAKEN.
teach.b: He comes back and speaks them aloud, one by one, and they share one shape.

When I become a Buddha, if my land still holds realms of suffering, may I not attain perfect awakening. When I become a Buddha, if the beings born there don't reach awakening, may I not attain it either. If not, not me.
In the version of the sutra read in China and Japan, there are forty-eight. Fourth, why the shape matters. The usual bargain says: first I'll get mine, then I'll help.
Dharmakara's vows run the other way, tying his own awakening to everyone else's. He refuses to count himself finished while the land he promised isn't real.
The sutra says the vows were fulfilled: he became a Buddha, and his land is the land of bliss. Who he became gets a day of its own.

how: Pure Land Buddhists chant and study the longer sutra on the land of bliss, in which the monk Dharmakara makes his vows; in East Asia the vows are counted as forty-eight, and temples and teachers return to them often.

s: Dharmakara started life as a monk
in the sutra he was a king who gave up his throne after hearing a Buddha teach.
Dharmakara's vows tie his own awakening to the welfare of others
each vow ends: if this is not so, may I not attain perfect awakening.
the version of the sutra read in China and Japan counts forty-eight vows
the version read in China and Japan lists forty-eight.

games.q: you're Dharmakara. your teacher has just shown you the lands of the Buddhas, the fine ones and the poor ones. what do you do?
o: choose the finest land and ask to be born there.
think it through for a very long time, then vow to make a land for everyone.
decide no land could ever be good enough.
games.why: in the sutra he goes quiet for an immense stretch of time, then makes his vows: a land built so others can awaken.

practice: Choose one small, concrete thing you'll do for someone else this week, a call, a ride, a meal, an hour of listening, and give it Dharmakara's shape in your own words: I won't call this week finished until it's done.
Say it once, silently, then breathe and let it settle, not as pressure but as a promise you've chosen.

wordCard.voice: The monk Dharmakara: a king who became a monk, studied the lands of the Buddhas, and vowed not to accept awakening unless his land would carry others to it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Dharmakara, rendered 'treasury of the dharma'. in Japanese he is Hozo (法蔵).

carryVoice: Your line: forty-eight vows. Each one ends the same way: if not, not me. Same time tomorrow.
